That vigor is useful in a contained planting but can become a nuisance in an open bed. Native to parts of Europe and the Mediterranean region, it has been grown and naturalized elsewhere; garden spread should be described separately from documented ecological harm.

proposedDescription: Apple of Peru has pale blue, bell-shaped flowers followed by fruit enclosed in a papery covering. This annual member of the nightshade family comes from South America and can grow quickly in fertile, disturbed ground. It spreads by seed and may appear as a garden escape or field weed. Despite the familiar-looking fruit covering, it should not be confused with edible groundcherries.
identification: Look for angular stems, broad unevenly toothed or lobed leaves, blue flowers with pale centers, and inflated fruit coverings.
actions: Avoid eating the fruits or other plant parts. If removing unwanted plants, act before mature seed is shed.

previousDescription: Apple of Peru looks at home in a flower border, with pale blue bells and a papery case around each fruit. It is a summer annual in the nightshade family, native to South America and naturalized in parts of the United States. Plants grow quickly in disturbed, fertile ground and spread by abundant seed. That combination has carried this ornamental into crop fields and other disturbed sites. Its lanternlike fruits can suggest an edible ground cherry, but the resemblance is misleading: this plant should not be treated as a food plant.

proposedDescription: Arabian jasmine is an evergreen shrub or scrambling climber with glossy, oval leaves and strongly scented white flowers. The flowers may turn pink as they age, and cultivated forms can have one or several layers of petals. Despite its name, its native range includes areas from Bhutan to India. It is widely grown in warm climates for its flowers and fragrance.
identification: Compare the glossy, simple leaves and fragrant white flowers; doubled cultivars can obscure normal flower structure.

previousDescription: Arabian jasmine is best known for the fragrance of its white flowers. This evergreen shrub can scramble over nearby support, carrying glossy oval leaves and blooms that may blush pink as they age. Cultivated forms range from simple flowers to richly doubled rosettes, so a garden specimen may look quite different from another plant of the same species. Despite its common name, Kew places its native range in Bhutan and India. Its long history in gardens and flower use is part of its story, but does not by itself demonstrate ecological harm where it has been introduced.

proposedDescription: Arabian schismus is a small annual grass with fine leaves and a short, compact flower head. It grows in dry, open places and disturbed desert ground. In the southwestern United States, its dried growth can help carry fire across spaces between shrubs, especially when seasons of abundant rain produce more vegetation. It closely resembles Schismus barbatus, another introduced desert grass. Small differences in the flower parts are more dependable for separating them than a photograph of their leaves.
identification: Examine mature flower parts with a regional grass key; a photograph of fine leaves alone is not reliable.

previousDescription: Arabian schismus is a small annual grass that grows in dry, open places. After rain, its fine leaves and stems can fill spaces between desert shrubs; when dry, that growth can help fire move through areas that once had little continuous fuel. Originally known from the Old World, it has also been documented in the Caribbean and Central America. It feeds on fungal growth and has sometimes damaged cultivated bracket fungi. Finding this insect around wood does not by itself show that a healthy tree is being attacked; its documented food is fungal tissue.
identification: A flattened brown bug around fungus-bearing wood needs expert comparison with other flat bugs.

Brachyrhynchus membranaceus has records in both the Old World and the Western Hemisphere, and has sometimes affected cultivated bracket fungi. Finding it in wood does not mean it is attacking a healthy tree; its feeding is associated with fungal growth.

proposedDescription: Araucaria aphid feeds on young growth of Araucaria trees, including around the bases of needles on fresh shoots. Wingless individuals are broadly oval and bright yellow to orange, measuring only about one to one and a half millimeters long. Their tiny size makes a close look worthwhile. The species has been recorded in several tropical and subtropical regions, but that wide distribution does not clearly identify its original home. The host and color are useful clues rather than a complete diagnosis.
identification: Check fresh Araucaria shoots for broad yellow to orange aphids; confirm with a specialist rather than relying on color.

proposedDescription: Araucaria black scale can look like a dark speck attached to a leaf. The female shelters beneath a nearly circular, flattened brown-black cover with darker shed skins near its center. Despite the name, its hosts extend well beyond Araucaria: palms, olives and many other woody plants have been recorded. This broad host range makes examination of the insect especially useful. A dark spot on a familiar plant can suggest an armored scale, but it does not establish this species.
identification: Inspect dark circular leaf scales with magnification; an adult female may need slide-mounted examination.

Like other armored scales, the insect spends much of its life protected beneath this cover, making the covering more visible than the animal itself.

proposedDescription: Arborescent pricklypear is a Mexican cactus that can grow into a large shrub or small tree. Its gray-green pads carry white hairs and spines, while older growth develops a trunk. Yellow flowers are followed by fleshy fruit. Broken pads can take root, allowing plants to spread from discarded garden material. It has escaped cultivation in places including Australia, where dense growth can become a management problem.
identification: Look for a trunked habit, finely hairy pads, and slender white spines; compare with similar prickly pears.
actions: Avoid spreading detached pads or dumping cactus material in natural areas. Use local disposal guidance and protect hands from spines and tiny barbed glochids.

previousDescription: Aaron's beard prickly pear can grow from a cluster of pads into a branching, trunked shrub. Its gray-green pads carry tiny pale hairs and flexible white spines, while yellow flowers are followed by fleshy fruit. Native to Mexico, it has escaped cultivation in parts of Australia, where managers document spread from detached plant pieces and dumped garden material. Those Australian impacts should not be assumed everywhere, but the way the plant travels is useful to understand. A broken pad can be more than waste: it may be the start of another plant.

proposedDescription: Argentine ants are small brown ants often seen moving in long, busy trails. They form networks of shallow nests with multiple queens and can spread through gardens, buildings and natural areas. Native to South America, they have become established in many other regions. They collect sugary honeydew from sap-feeding insects and can displace other ants where their colonies become dominant.
identification: Workers are uniformly dull brown, about 1/8 inch long, with one waist node; confirm against other small household ants.
actions: Follow trails to locate entry points and nests, confirm the ant, and use local species-appropriate bait guidance if control is needed.

researchNotes: UC IPM identification account and Texas A&M biology and management account read. Bait advice is conditional on confirmed identification; no blanket outdoor spraying advice.
previousDescription: A busy ribbon of small brown ants along a wall or garden path may belong to Argentine ants. Workers are similar in size and move between shallow nests that can form part of a much larger network with many queens. Originally South American, this ant has become established in other regions and readily uses gardens and buildings. It feeds on sweet foods and tends honeydew-producing insects, which can complicate garden pest management. A trail in the kitchen is usually only the visible end of activity that extends outdoors.

proposedDescription: Argentine black and white tegu is a large, strong-bodied lizard with a banded tail. Young animals often have greenish heads. It eats a wide range of foods and can shelter in burrows during cold weather. Established populations in Florida are a concern because tegus eat native wildlife, including eggs and young animals; documented prey include alligator eggs and young gopher tortoises.
identification: Look for a large, sturdy black-and-white lizard with a long banded tail; young animals may have a green head.
actions: In Florida, photograph a suspected tegu, record the location, and report it to FWC. Never release a pet; use an approved surrender option instead.

previousDescription: The Argentine black and white tegu is a large, ground-dwelling South American lizard with a banded or mottled body and a powerful tail. Young tegus often have green heads that fade as they grow. Adults eat a varied diet of fruit, insects, eggs, and small animals, and retreat into burrows during colder weather. In Florida, established populations raise conservation concerns because researchers have documented predation on native wildlife, including alligator eggs and young gopher tortoises. Its adaptable habits help explain why an escaped pet can become more than an isolated garden visitor.

proposedDescription: Argentine pepperweed is a hairy member of the mustard family with divided lower leaves and simpler leaves higher on the stem. Its small white flowers develop into flattened pods with a notch at the tip. The lower leaves may disappear as the plant matures, changing its overall appearance. Looking at both the remaining leaves and the seed pods helps distinguish it from other pepperweeds.
identification: Photograph lower and upper leaves, stem hairs, and ripe pods; compare with other Lepidium species.

previousDescription: Argentine pepperweed is a small mustard relative whose seedpods are often easier to recognize than its tiny flowers. Lower leaves are deeply divided, while the leaves higher on a flowering stem become simpler. Hairy stems carry little pale flowers followed by flattened, rounded pods with a notch at the tip. Plants can look quite different as they mature and lose their lower leaves, so a complete photograph is more useful than a single flower. Records of naturalization describe where it grows outside its original range; they do not alone measure ecological damage.

proposedDescription: Aonidiella taxus is an armored scale found on yews, plum-yews and Podocarpus. A pale, partly transparent cover hides the reddish female beneath it, often on the underside of a leaf. Feeding can leave yellow patches around the insects. Its life also involves much smaller visitors: researchers in Japan found several kinds of tiny wasps parasitizing this scale. The cover and host plant offer useful clues, but related scales can look alike and a confident species identification requires microscopic examination.
identification: Inspect needle and leaf undersides for pale rounded scales and nearby yellowing; slide-mounted females are needed for confirmation.
actions: Avoid moving a suspect infested plant into a collection until its scales are identified.

Feeding on leaf undersides can be associated with yellow patches. The young insects are mobile before settling down, and infested nursery plants can carry them to new locations even when the small scales are not immediately obvious.

proposedDescription: Arborvitae scale is a tiny armored insect associated with arborvitae, junipers and other conifers. Its cover can be oval or almost round, with a dull greenish-yellow color that becomes paler and browner with age. Infestations may accompany discolored foliage and dying twigs. A Pennsylvania study found a small parasitic wasp attacking this scale, and predatory mites sheltering in the empty scale covers afterward. Those observations reveal a small community around the insect, but do not establish a tested treatment for an infested tree.
identification: Look for pale yellowish armored scales on conifers; distinguish them from similar scales through expert examination.

Natural enemies include tiny wasps and mites, although their presence does not guarantee that a particular infestation will remain harmless.

proposedDescription: Gymnaspis aechmeae is a tiny armored scale sometimes called flyspeck scale. Its dark covering can resemble a speck of dirt on bromeliads and other ornamental plants, including those grown in greenhouses. The female remains within the skin from an earlier growth stage and produces live young that can crawl to new feeding sites. Infested plants provide a route for it to move between locations.
identification: Examine persistent dark specks on bromeliad leaves with magnification; confirm they are scales and have the species identified.

previousDescription: Fly speck scale is aptly named: on a bromeliad, its small dark coverings can be mistaken for dirt. The insect has become a pest of bromeliad collections and greenhouse plants, where colonies can spoil the appearance of leaves. Mature females remain within a shed skin and produce mobile young rather than laying exposed eggs. Those crawlers can move between nearby plants, while the trade in living plants can carry the species much farther. Its native range is uncertain, so a precise origin story would overstate what the available evidence establishes.

Researchers studying Mexican avocado orchards found it singly or in very small groups on branches, sometimes alongside other armored scales. Despite its common name, the exact way it becomes covered by plant tissue is not well understood, so it is better described as concealed than as a proven tunneling insect.

This unusual feature has led to the name mining scale, although it is not a leaf-mining insect. It feeds on a range of woody plants. Because the covering blends into the plant surface, colonies may be less noticeable than exposed scales on leaves or stems.

Its covers can look much like those of other Lepidosaphes scales. A close view helps locate the insects, while microscopic features of the female are needed to distinguish similar species reliably.

Lepidosaphes yanagicola also uses other deciduous trees and shrubs, including willow, maple and elm. Adult females can survive the winter and produce eggs the following summer. Heavy infestations sometimes accompany early leaf fall and twig dieback, although damage varies among locations. proposedDescription: Harper scale can blend into bark even when several insects are present. Its narrow, nearly flat tan covers are only about one to two millimeters long, with darker shed skins at one end and a pink or red female underneath. It feeds on a variety of woody plants and often settles in bark cracks. A specialist comparing specimens from California, Japan and Taiwan confirmed how widely the same species had been recorded. Its sheltered position and resemblance to other scales make microscopic examination important for a reliable identification.
identification: Examine bark cracks in good light for narrow tan scales; reliable species identification requires microscopic examination.

Its narrow, fairly flat cover is tan with a darker end, concealing a pinkish female underneath. The insect is only around one to two millimeters long. proposedDescription: Parlatoria camelliae is an armored scale found on camellias and other hosts. Its pale to gray covering has a darker patch made from earlier shed skins. Colonies can occur on either side of a leaf, often near veins, and feeding may discolor the foliage. Reports from places such as Galicia document its presence, but identification still requires attention to the insect rather than leaf discoloration alone.
identification: Inspect both leaf surfaces, especially near veins, and distinguish this species from tea scale and other camellia scales.

previousDescription: Camellia parlatoria scale settles on leaves as small pale to grayish covers with a darker patch of shed skin. It has been recorded from more hosts than its common name suggests. Observations on camellia found insects on both leaf surfaces, often near veins; researchers in Galicia also documented discoloration on affected plants. Such marks can prompt a closer look, but leaf discoloration has many causes and several scale species share camellias. The insect under the cover, rather than the plant's symptoms alone, is what allows a specialist to identify it.

proposedDescription: Rutherfordia major is an armored scale associated with lychee and other tropical woody plants. Its initially pale covering may become covered by plant tissue and appear reddish or dark, helping it blend into bark. It has been introduced to places including the Galapagos. Movement of host plants is relevant to its spread, while the full history of its original distribution remains less certain.
identification: Look for rounded to oval covers partly hidden by tissue, with brown shed skins near the edge; specialist confirmation is needed.

previousDescription: Lychee bark scale can be difficult to recognize because its normally white cover becomes obscured by plant tissue. The resulting patch may look reddish brown or almost black rather than snowy white. The insect uses a range of tropical woody hosts, not only lychee. Records from the Galapagos describe an established introduction associated with plant material, while older literature discusses possible importance on lychee in Florida. These are different kinds of evidence: an introduced population is not, by itself, proof of a measured ecological impact.

proposedDescription: Selenaspidus albus is an armored scale with a small white disk for a cover. Slightly off-center, yellow-brown remains of earlier growth stages form a contrasting patch. The female's cover is usually less than two millimeters across, making a single insect easy to overlook. Euphorbia is a documented host, and crowded colonies have been reported on cultivated plants. A British botanical-garden report also found a heavy infestation on an imported Euphorbia kept in a heated glasshouse.
identification: Examine white circular covers on Euphorbia with magnification; the off-center shed skins help detection but do not confirm the species.

The covering is less than two millimeters across, so individual insects are easy to overlook; heavier colonies are more conspicuous and can warrant closer inspection of the host plant.

Each female's cover has a pale edge and an off-center patch of darker shed skins. Citrus is a frequent host, but Selenaspidus articulatus feeds on many other plants, including rubber trees. Dense populations can cause yellowing and damaged leaf or fruit tissue. A field study in Brazil found that numbers on rubber trees changed with the season and differed among tree clones, so infestation levels should be assessed in their local setting.

actions: Avoid transporting visibly infested plants and obtain a confirmed identification before selecting control.

proposedDescription: Unaspis citri is often noticed as a snowy white coating on citrus trunks and branches. That appearance comes largely from the white covers of immature males; females have darker, shell-shaped covers. Heavy feeding can weaken trees, contribute to branch dieback and cause bark to split. Its concentration on woody parts of the tree helps distinguish citrus snow scale from some scales found mainly on leaves.

Colonies are usually concentrated on citrus bark and larger limbs, with leaves and fruit involved when infestations are severe. Persistent heavy feeding can weaken a tree and contribute to branch dieback and splitting bark. Inspecting both the white male covers and the less noticeable females gives a much clearer picture than looking only for a white coating.

Its brown, elongated covering resembles a small shell on woody hosts, including lychee. Heavy populations may reduce plant vigor or damage branches. Changes in the scientific name can make records harder to connect, so both names are useful when checking the research behind an identification.

The old name is worth retaining in a search, but a scale on lychee should still be identified carefully: several armored scales can share the crop and look like small pieces of bark.

Dense colonies may also leave white secretions on the leaves. The 'snout' is a much smaller feature of the female's head, visible with close microscopic study. Several related Fiorinia species look similar in the field, so the shape of a brown cover alone is not a reliable identification.

Tiny rounded spikelets sit in paired rows along those branches, a useful detail for identification. Paspalum paniculatum grows in disturbed clearings and other open ground. Its home range includes tropical America, while regional floras record it as introduced elsewhere, including the United States and Australia; a local record needs that regional context.
identification: Photograph a complete mature seed head and the arrangement of spikelets; leaf shape alone is insufficient.

proposedDescription: Arrow bamboo has upright canes and long, broad leaves that make it popular as a screen. Beneath the soil, spreading stems can carry new shoots well beyond the original planting. It can form dense patches where it escapes cultivation. Records from places including Maryland and New Zealand illustrate why its underground growth matters when assessing a planting near neighboring gardens or natural vegetation.
identification: Compare broad elongated leaves, cane sheaths, and spreading rhizomes with other running bamboos.
actions: Check the edge of a planting for new shoots and seek local bamboo-management guidance before removal; ordinary lawn broadleaf weed treatments do not target bamboo.

previousDescription: Arrow bamboo forms a leafy screen of upright canes and long, broad green leaves. What happens below ground is just as important: running underground stems can send new shoots beyond the original planting. That habit has helped it escape gardens, with naturalized stands described beside rivers, roads, and woodland edges in New Zealand and reports of invasive growth in Maryland. An established patch is therefore more than the canes you can see. Identification and a plan for the underground growth are useful before attempting to remove or contain it.

proposedDescription: Arrowleaf elephant ear has large, arrow-shaped leaves held on long stalks that meet the leaf at its base. Thick underground growth and new shoots help it expand into patches. It favors warm, moist places and can grow along streams. In parts of Florida, escaped plants are considered invasive, where their large leaves and dense growth can crowd other vegetation.
identification: Look at the stalk attachment at the leaf base and the broad arrow-shaped blade; compare with Colocasia and native Peltandra before removal.
actions: Prevent a cultivated patch from escaping and avoid dumping live underground pieces near wetlands. Confirm identification before disturbing a wild patch.

previousDescription: Arrowleaf elephant's ear makes a bold patch of tropical greenery, with large arrow-shaped leaves held on long stalks. The stalk joins the blade at its base, a useful clue when comparing plants commonly called elephant ears. Thick underground growth produces offsets, allowing colonies to expand in moist places such as streambanks. It has a long history as a cultivated tropical plant, but it can also escape. Florida assessments describe invasive behavior in some regions, where dense growth can crowd or shade native vegetation; those regional findings should not be treated as a universal status.

proposedDescription: Artist's pallet is grown for its heart- to arrow-shaped leaves, patterned in combinations of green, white, pink and red. It grows from underground tubers and produces small flowers grouped on a fleshy spike within a pale surrounding leaf-like structure. Native to tropical America, it is widely cultivated. Its colorful foliage is ornamental rather than edible, and the plant's tissues can cause irritation.
identification: Look for colorful arrow- or heart-shaped leaves with the stalk joining inside the blade; cultivated hybrids can complicate species identification.
actions: Keep the plant from being eaten and avoid contact with sap when handling damaged leaves or tubers.

previousDescription: Caladium is grown for leaves that can look hand-painted in green, white, pink, and red. The broad blades range from heart-shaped to arrow-shaped and rise on long stalks from underground tubers. Its flowers are much less conspicuous, carried on a fleshy spike within a pale bract. This tropical American plant is widely cultivated, with garden forms that vary greatly in color and shape. An ornamental caladium should not automatically be described as an invasive threat, but its sap and tissues do deserve care around people and pets because they contain irritating compounds.

proposedDescription: Diplosoma listerianum is a colonial sea squirt that forms thin, soft sheets over submerged surfaces. Many tiny filtering animals share the same gelatinous covering. Colonies grow on docks, boat hulls and natural surfaces, giving them opportunities to travel with marine traffic. They can cover other organisms as they spread, but the long history of transport makes the species' original native range difficult to establish.
identification: Look for a very thin, translucent colony with tiny individual openings and larger shared outlets; confirm with a marine specialist.

previousDescription: What looks like a thin gelatinous film on a dock or boat hull may be a colony of tiny sea squirts. In Diplosoma listerianum, many individuals share a soft outer covering, drawing in seawater and filtering suspended food. Colonies spread across submerged surfaces rather than moving around as adults. That makes boat hulls and other fouled equipment important to its story. Similar sheet-forming tunicates can be difficult to separate by eye, and the species' long history of transport complicates claims about where every population originated.

proposedDescription: Polyandrocarpa zorritensis is a colonial sea squirt made up of small, club-shaped individuals connected by root-like strands. Each has its own outer covering and two openings used in filter feeding. Colonies occur on docks, boats and natural surfaces such as mangrove roots, and can overgrow neighboring organisms. It was described from Peru, but that alone does not establish where it originally evolved.
identification: Look for separate club-shaped individuals joined at their bases, sometimes coated with sand; distinguish from tunicates that form a continuous flat sheet.

previousDescription: This sea squirt grows as a cluster of small, club-shaped animals, joined at their bases by rootlike strands. Each individual has its own tough covering and two openings through which it pumps and filters seawater. Colonies occur on docks, boat hulls, and natural surfaces such as mangroves. Introduced populations have been documented in several regions, and some colonies can overgrow other organisms. Its original home remains uncertain in the Smithsonian account, despite having first been described from Peru; the place where a species was named is not necessarily its native range. Experiments also show that salinity can limit its asexual reproduction, so success in one harbor does not predict equal growth in another.

proposedDescription: Ash whitefly feeds beneath the leaves of trees and shrubs, including pears, pomegranates and citrus. Adults are small and white; immature insects have distinctive waxy structures and may carry tiny droplets. Feeding and honeydew can harm foliage and encourage sooty mold. In California, introduced natural enemies greatly reduced a once-serious outbreak, making this species a notable example of successful biological control.
identification: Inspect leaf undersides for immatures with a wax band and droplet-tipped projections; flying white adults alone are not diagnostic.
actions: Check for natural enemies before treating. Avoid disrupting effective biological control with unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides.

previousDescription: Ash whitefly can cover the undersides of leaves with tiny sap-feeding insects. Adults are pale and wax-dusted, but the settled young are more distinctive, with a thick wax band and a fringe of fine tubes ending in droplets. Ash is only one host; pears, pomegranates, citrus, and other broadleaved trees can also support it. Heavy infestations can leave sticky honeydew and harm foliage or fruit. Its history in California also shows the value of natural enemies: introduced parasitoids greatly reduced a once conspicuous pest problem.

proposedDescription: Ashy cinquefoil has small yellow flowers and leaves divided into five to seven toothed leaflets. Pale hairs on the undersides give the foliage a grayish cast, and hairy stems rise above the lower leaves. It favors dry, open places, including roadsides, grasslands and disturbed ground. This Eurasian plant has been introduced to parts of North America. Several yellow-flowered cinquefoils look similar, so the leaflet shape, gray undersides and hairs around the flowers are more useful together than flower color alone.
identification: Compare both sides of the leaflets and the hairs on stems, sepals, and the small bracts beneath flowers; check against Potentilla intermedia.

Young animals have bold bands and bright reddish tails; adults become tan to rusty brown with pale speckling. Sphaerodactylus elegans has been introduced to Florida, where other small geckos can complicate identification. Observations from Cuba also describe these geckos hunting flies and ants around a house during daylight. Their changing colors and secretive habits make a clear photograph more useful than a fleeting glimpse.

The change in pattern as it grows means young and adult animals may look surprisingly different.

Slender stalks lift rounded, button-like flower heads above the foliage; these may look gray, yellowish or greenish rather than showy. identification: Examine a mature seed head and individual spikelets with magnification; do not identify it from leaf color or common name.

proposedDescription: Asian bush mosquito has pale-banded legs and golden markings on its back. It uses small pools of water, including rock pools, tree holes, tires and other containers, and can thrive in relatively cool, wooded settings near homes. Its ability to use artificial containers helps it spread. The species can carry pathogens under some conditions, but finding it does not establish local disease transmission.
identification: Golden thorax markings and banded legs suggest the species, but separation from other Aedes mosquitoes requires close examination.
actions: Empty, cover, or remove unnecessary water-holding containers. Use personal bite protection and local mosquito-control guidance for water that cannot be drained.

previousDescription: Asian bush mosquito develops in small collections of water, from rock pools and tree holes to discarded tires and garden containers. Adults have golden markings on the upper body and pale bands on their dark legs. The species tolerates cooler conditions than many familiar container mosquitoes, helping it use wooded and residential settings. Females take blood meals, but a mosquito's capacity to carry a virus in a laboratory should not be confused with proof that it is causing local disease transmission. Around a home, reducing water-holding containers is a practical way to reduce breeding opportunities.

proposedDescription: Asian chestnut gall wasp causes rounded swellings on the buds, leaves and shoots of true chestnut trees. These galls start green or pink and later become woody and brown, sometimes remaining after the wasps have left. Heavy infestations can reduce shoot growth and nut production. The adult wasp is tiny, so the galls are usually the first sign people notice.
identification: Look for rounded swellings on Castanea leaves and young shoots; distinguish fresh soft galls from old dry ones.
actions: Have unusual chestnut galls identified and seek local guidance before pruning or treatment. Avoid moving suspect nursery plants to new sites.

Rounded green or pink galls develop on chestnut buds, leaves, and shoots, sheltering the larvae inside. Later, the galls turn brown and woody and may remain attached after the insects have left. Repeated gall formation can disrupt growth and flowering and reduce nut production. This pest attacks true chestnuts in Castanea, and its management has included carefully studied biological control; an old gall is not proof that a living wasp is still inside.

proposedDescription: Asian citrus psyllid is a small sap-feeding insect often seen with its body tilted upward as it feeds on tender citrus growth. Young insects are yellow-orange and produce curled, waxy tubes. Feeding can distort new leaves, but its greater importance is its ability to transmit the bacteria associated with citrus greening disease. Identifying the insect accurately helps distinguish that risk from ordinary leaf damage.
identification: Check tender citrus shoots for tilted mottled-brown adults, yellowish young, and curly white wax; confirm suspect insects or disease symptoms.
actions: Report suspected psyllids or citrus-greening symptoms through local agricultural authorities where reporting is requested. Do not move suspect citrus plants or cuttings while seeking guidance.

previousDescription: Asian citrus psyllid often feeds with its rear end raised from a citrus leaf, giving the tiny insect a distinctive tilted posture. Yellow-orange young cluster on tender growth and produce curled white wax tubes. Feeding can distort shoots, but the greater concern is transmission of the bacteria associated with huanglongbing, or citrus greening. Infected trees can decline and produce poor fruit, and there is no cure for the disease. A psyllid sighting does not prove a tree is infected, but it is a good reason to follow local citrus plant-health guidance promptly.

proposedDescription: Asian cockroach usually lives outdoors in leaf litter, mulch and similar sheltered places. proposedDescription: Asiatic clam has a rounded, roughly triangular shell marked by strong concentric ridges, usually yellowish to brown. It filters tiny particles from freshwater and can also feed on organic material in the sediment. Rapid growth and reproduction can build dense populations that alter food and nutrient conditions. Large numbers may clog water intakes. Effects on native mussels vary among places, so the presence of this clam alone does not establish why a native population has declined.

It filters particles from the water and can reach high densities, changing food and nutrient conditions and competing with native mussels. Large populations may also clog water-intake equipment, making it important to both aquatic ecosystems and water infrastructure.

proposedDescription: Asiatic dayflower opens vivid blue flowers that usually last only a day. Each flower has two large blue petals and a much smaller pale one. Its leaves wrap around the stems, which can take root where they touch the ground. Native to East Asia, it grows in disturbed places and can become a crop weed, spreading through patches of moist, suitable soil.

previousDescription: Asiatic dayflower is a sprawling annual whose bright blue flowers open for only a day. Two large blue petals sit above a much smaller pale petal, while smooth, pointed leaves wrap around the stem in a sheath. Stems touching the ground can root and help a patch spread. Originally from eastern Asia, it now grows in fields, gardens, and other disturbed places. It can compete with crops or nearby vegetation, and its ability to survive some common herbicides makes correct identification useful.

proposedDescription: Asiatic dock has large lower leaves and upright flowering stems that rise above the surrounding vegetation. It grows along rivers, in meadows and in disturbed ground, where seeds and spreading underground stems can help it form patches. Research in Central Europe found that light and shallow burial strongly influenced seedling emergence, helping explain establishment in gaps and disturbed soil. It has expanded in parts of Europe, but those regional findings do not establish its effects in every place it occurs.

proposedDescription: Asiatic garden beetle is a small, cinnamon-brown beetle with a rounded shape resembling a coffee bean. Adults hide during the day and feed on leaves at night. Underground, the pale, C-shaped grubs feed on roots and can damage seedlings. Introduced from Asia, it occurs in the United States, where the larvae have also become a concern in some corn-growing areas.

previousDescription: Asiatic garden beetle is a small cinnamon-brown scarab with the rounded shape of a coffee bean. Adults hide during the day and emerge at night to chew leaves; their pale, C-shaped grubs feed underground on roots and young seedlings. Both stages use many garden and crop plants. Introduced from Asia, it has caused damaging infestations in some U.S. corn fields as well as landscapes. This two-part life cycle explains why ragged foliage and weak seedlings can point to the same insect.

proposedDescription: Asiatic witchweed is a parasitic plant that attaches to the roots of grasses, including crops such as corn and sorghum. Its narrow, hairy leaves and small flowers appear above ground, while the connection to its host remains hidden below. Seeds can persist in soil for a long time. That persistence helps explain the long-running monitoring and control efforts around infestations in the Carolinas.

previousDescription: Asiatic witchweed is a small flowering plant with narrow leaves, coarse hairs, and flowers that may be red, yellow, white, or purple. Much of its effect begins before it appears above ground: the young plant attaches to grass roots and draws resources from its host. Crops such as corn and sorghum can be badly weakened. Its dustlike seeds can remain in soil for years, which is why introduced populations in the Carolinas have required persistent monitoring and control rather than a single season of weeding.

proposedDescription: Asparagus beetle is a small, dark beetle with pale spots and reddish edges. Both adults and grayish larvae feed on asparagus. Dark eggs are often laid upright on the plant, and feeding can scar spears or strip foliage. It differs from the orange, spotted asparagus beetle, so noticing the adult's color pattern helps connect damage with the correct species.

previousDescription: Common asparagus beetle is a small, dark beetle marked with pale spots and reddish edges. Both adults and their plump grayish larvae feed on asparagus, while rows of upright, dark eggs may be visible on the spears. Feeding can scar the edible shoots and damage the leafy summer growth that supports the next crop. The orange, black-spotted asparagus beetle is a different species. Checking the adult's markings and the affected plant parts helps connect a beetle sighting with the damage in a garden.

proposedDescription: Asparagus fern is a flowering plant with fine, feathery-looking growth. The narrow green structures that resemble leaves are modified stems; its true leaves are much smaller. True Asparagus densiflorus has upright, closely branched growth, with small white to pinkish flowers that can develop into red berries. It grows naturally on sandy ground in southeastern Africa. Garden names are often mixed with Asparagus aethiopicus, so an arching plant sold as a Sprengeri asparagus fern may represent that related species instead.

Names are sometimes confused with the related Asparagus aethiopicus, so garden labels alone may not establish the exact species.

The insect also pupates within its mine before emerging as a tiny moth. These altered patches on leaves are often easier to notice than the adults; a leaf mine still needs careful identification because other insects make similar marks.

proposedDescription: This asthmaweed, Conyza bonariensis, is an annual or short-lived plant with narrow, hairy, gray-green leaves. Its many small flower heads release seeds carried by fine, fluffy hairs. Originally from South America, it grows in fields, orchards and along roads in other regions. Wind dispersal helps it reach newly disturbed ground, where a small plant can develop into a much-branched seed producer.

previousDescription: Hairy fleabane, also called asthmaweed, is a fast-growing annual or biennial with narrow leaves and a covering of grayish hairs. Branching stems carry many small flower heads that develop fluffy, wind-carried seeds. It grows in orchards, fields, roadsides, and other open, disturbed places. Native to South America, it has become a widespread agricultural weed elsewhere, where it competes for water and other resources. Its hairy foliage and branching pattern help separate it from similar fleabanes, though close comparisons are often needed.

Narrow leaves and the nearly hairless bracts around the heads help distinguish this species from some similar fleabanes. Its small fruits carry fine, pale bristles. It grows in disturbed places, including roadsides and river margins. Modern treatments place Conyza floribunda in Erigeron as Erigeron floribundus; older records sometimes mix it with E. sumatrensis, so those records need a name check.

proposedDescription: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen tree with fine, jointed-looking branches and tiny, scale-like leaves. Its deep roots and tolerance of dry, salty conditions have made it useful for shelter plantings. Outside cultivation, it can spread along waterways. In parts of Australia, dense stands have altered river habitats and soil conditions, showing how a tree valued for protection from wind can become a problem in the wrong setting.

previousDescription: Athel tamarisk is a large evergreen shrub or tree with a spreading crown and fine, jointed branchlets. Its tiny leaves hug the twigs, and clusters of pale pink to white flowers appear among the foliage. Deep roots and tolerance of drought and salty soils made it useful for shade and shelter in dry landscapes. It can also escape cultivation. In parts of Australia, dense riverbank infestations have altered water flow and soil salinity, illustrating why a hardy planted tree can become a management concern in some settings.

proposedDescription: Atlantic ivy is an evergreen vine that can carpet the ground or climb trees. Young growth has lobed leaves, while mature flowering growth has less-divided leaves and produces fruit eaten by birds. Stems can also root as they spread. Introduced populations in the Pacific Northwest can dominate forest ground cover and add weight to trees. It is closely related to, but distinct from, English ivy.

previousDescription: Atlantic ivy, often called Irish ivy, is an evergreen climbing vine that can also make a thick carpet across the ground. Young shoots carry lobed leaves; flowering shoots have less-divided leaves and produce berries. Rooting stems expand a patch locally, while birds can carry seeds farther away. In invaded Pacific Northwest woodlands, dense ivy can cover native understory plants and add weight to trees. It closely resembles English ivy, and the species or cultivar should be confirmed when interpreting local weed guidance.

proposedDescription: Aucuba whitefly is a tiny sap-feeding insect that uses many host plants, including citrus and ivy. Its dark, oval immature stages sit on leaves and are easier to examine with magnification. Plants moved through trade can carry it between locations. A California assessment reported no significant known impacts at that time, so detection should be distinguished from evidence of serious damage.

Its immature stages stay on leaves; the late immature cases are small, dark, and oval, and reliable identification requires magnification. Trade in infested plants can move it between regions. California's 2022 assessment reported no known significant economic or environmental damage there, while European observations likewise found limited injury. Finding the insect and demonstrating damage to its host are separate questions.

proposedDescription: Australasian geranium is a low-growing perennial with hairy, rounded leaves divided into lobes. Its small pink flowers have paler centers and usually appear singly or in pairs. Thickened roots support the plant in moist places such as gullies, creek margins and forested ground. The modest flowers and creeping or spreading growth can make it less conspicuous than familiar garden geraniums.

previousDescription: Australasian geranium is a low, sprawling perennial with coarse hairs and rounded leaves cut into several broad lobes. Small flowers, pink toward the tips and paler at the base, appear singly or in pairs. A thickened, branching root supports growth from season to season. In Australia it is associated with moist places such as creek banks, wet gullies, and forest margins. Its modest flowers and leaf shape help distinguish it from the more conspicuous plants commonly sold as garden geraniums.

proposedDescription: Australian backyard mosquito has white-banded legs, a pale ring on its mouthparts and lyre-shaped markings on its back. It breeds in small water collections, including tree holes and containers around homes. Adults may bite during the day in shaded places. Originally associated with Australasia, it has also been detected in California, where container habitats can provide suitable places for it to reproduce.

previousDescription: Australian backyard mosquito is a dark mosquito with white-banded legs, pale lyre-shaped markings on its back, and a white ring around the middle of its long feeding tube. Its young use tree holes and rain-filled containers, including plant trays, buckets, and drains. Females bite people and other animals, sometimes during the day in shade. Recent detections in California show how this adaptable mosquito can become a neighborhood concern. Its markings matter because it closely resembles other introduced Aedes mosquitoes.

proposedDescription: Australian brake is a fern with large fronds divided into many narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short base, and lines of spore-producing structures form along the undersides of the leaf edges. It grows naturally in Australasian forest and stream habitats and is also cultivated. Looking beneath a mature frond can reveal features that are less obvious from its overall shape.

previousDescription: Australian brake is a large, lacy fern whose fronds divide repeatedly into narrow green segments. Brown stalks rise from a short, scaly base, and the fronds can move delicately in a breeze. Lines of spore-producing structures run near the underside edges of fertile segments. It grows in sheltered forest, streamside, and garden settings and has been cultivated beyond its Australasian range. Looking beneath a frond provides useful identification details that are easy to miss when seeing only its feathery outline.

proposedDescription: Australian cheesewood is an evergreen tree with glossy, wavy-edged leaves and fragrant white flowers. Orange capsules open to expose sticky seeds that birds can carry away. Native to eastern Australia, it has become weedy in some places outside its natural range. Its attractive foliage and scent explain its garden use, while bird-dispersed seeds help it move beyond planted sites.

previousDescription: Australian cheesewood, or sweet pittosporum, is a shrub or tree with glossy leaves edged in gentle waves. Fragrant creamy-white flowers are followed by orange to yellow-brown capsules that open around sticky seeds. Birds help move those seeds away from planted trees. Although native to parts of eastern Australia, it has spread beyond its earlier range and become an environmental weed in some Australian forests and coastal scrub. Its familiar garden appearance can therefore mean different things depending on the local setting.

proposedDescription: Australian eelgrass is a freshwater plant with long, ribbon-like leaves rooted in the bottom. It spreads through runners and can form dense underwater beds. Female flowers reach the surface, and their stalks coil after pollination. Despite the common name, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations occur in places including California's Delta, where its underwater growth can change the structure of aquatic habitat.

Underground runners connect neighboring plants into tall underwater meadows. Small female flowers reach the surface on slender stalks, which coil back underwater after pollination. Despite the name eelgrass, it is not a marine seagrass. Introduced populations have been documented in California's Sacramento-San Joaquin Delta, where distinguishing it from other ribbonlike aquatic plants helps track changes in submerged vegetation.

proposedDescription: Australian fingergrass is easiest to recognize by its little windmill-shaped seed heads. Usually six to nine slender branches spread almost horizontally from the top of a stem, with the florets turning dark as they mature. Narrow leaves form a low, dense clump beneath flowering stems that can reach about knee height. Native to Australia, it grows on varied soils and flowers in response to rain. The detached seed heads can tumble in the wind, helping scatter seed.

It forms low clumps with narrow leaves, and the flowering branches darken as they mature. Native to Australia, it responds to rainfall and grows on a range of soils. The spoke-like head is its clearest feature when seen among other grasses.

It is native to eastern and southeastern Australia, where it grows in woodland and pasture settings. It should not be confused with other lovegrasses that have different ranges and impacts.

Narrow leaves sit below an open, branching flower head made of many small, neatly stacked spikelets. A tiny fringe of hairs where the leaf meets the stem provides another identification clue. Native to eastern and southeastern Australia, it occurs in woodland and native pasture. Several unrelated concerns are attached to other plants called lovegrass, so the scientific name matters when deciding what a local observation means.

Older trees develop rough bark and may have broad buttresses at the base. Woody fruits release winged seeds. Its valuable timber led to extensive historical logging, and trees growing in open sites can look quite different from tall forest-grown specimens.

New foliage can flush reddish pink, while mature trunks develop scaly bark and substantial buttress roots. Small pale flowers are followed by woody capsules that release winged seeds. Its rich-colored, workable timber made it historically valuable and led to extensive logging in Australia. The shape also changes with its surroundings: forest trees can grow tall and straight, while open-grown trees develop broader spreading crowns.

It comes from northern Australia and nearby regions, using streams, lakes and seasonally changing waters. Widely farmed for food, it can escape cultivation. It eats a variety of plant and animal material, making its establishment relevant to the waters and species it encounters.

Mature males have a soft, bright red patch along the outer edge of each large claw, a useful identification clue. It uses tropical streams, lakes, and billabongs in its native northern Australian range and is also farmed for food. It eats a varied diet that includes naturally occurring pond organisms and plant material. Movement for aquaculture has taken it beyond its home waters, where escaped populations can interact with local species.

proposedDescription: Australian saltbush is a low, spreading plant that can form a mat over dry or salty ground. Its gray-green leaves have a fine coating, especially beneath, and its seed-bearing structures become fleshy and red. It has been planted for forage and erosion control. Animals can spread its seeds, and it has established outside cultivation in places including coastal California.

Small gray-green leaves often look dusted underneath, and the seed is enclosed in fleshy reddish structures. Native to Australia, it was introduced elsewhere for uses including forage and erosion control. It tolerates dry and salty ground and has colonized disturbed coastal habitats in California. Animals can carry its seeds, helping explain how a plant close to the ground can establish new patches some distance away.

proposedDescription: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers and persistent woody seed capsules. Older plants may have twisted trunks and textured bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it has been planted as a screen and windbreak and has become invasive in some other regions. Newer botanical references may list it as Gaudium laevigatum rather than Leptospermum laevigatum.

previousDescription: Australian teatree is a shrub or small tree with gray-green leaves, white flowers, and flat-topped woody seed capsules. Older plants can develop wonderfully twisted trunks and shaggy bark. Native to coastal southeastern Australia, it tolerates salt spray and has been planted as a screen or windbreak. It has also naturalized beyond its original range and become weedy in some regions. Recent botanical treatments may use Gaudium laevigatum, so both names are helpful when matching observations with planting records or identification guides.

proposedDescription: Australian tortoise beetle is a rounded brown beetle, often mottled with darker marks, that feeds on eucalyptus. Adults and larvae chew the leaves, leaving curved or semicircular notches along the edges. Adults commonly feed at night and shelter beneath loose bark during the day, a habit also documented in Chilean field collections. Introduced populations occur in California. Established, well-cared-for trees often tolerate feeding, although heavy defoliation can add stress; finding beetles does not by itself show how seriously a tree is affected.

proposedDescription: Australian tubeworm lives inside a hard, pale tube attached to a submerged surface. A feathery crown reaches into the water to collect tiny food particles, then withdraws into the tube when disturbed. It favors sheltered brackish places such as estuaries, lagoons and docks. Many generations can build tangled, reef-like colonies, although reefs do not form everywhere it occurs. It also grows on boat hulls and structures. Despite its common name, an Australian native origin remains uncertain.

previousDescription: Australian tubeworm builds hard, pale tubes in brackish water. It also grows on boats and marine infrastructure, which can help it travel. Despite its common name, its original native range is uncertain; the name should not be treated as proof of an Australian origin.

proposedDescription: Australian waterbuttons is a small, low-growing plant with finely divided leaves and tiny flower heads that look like buttons. The heads are cream to pale yellow and lack the showy outer petals of many daisies. Slender stems may lie along the ground or turn upward, and can root where they touch suitable soil. Look for it in lawns, roadsides, open grassland and other disturbed places. Its modest size can make the button heads easier to notice than the plant beneath them.

proposedDescription: Austrian pine has stiff, dark green needles held in pairs. Young trees are often roughly pyramid-shaped, while older trees develop broader crowns, deeply furrowed bark and brown cones. Native across parts of Europe, northwestern Africa and western Asia, it has been widely planted for screens and windbreaks. Its paired needles and mature bark are useful features when comparing it with other planted pines.

previousDescription: Austrian pine is a substantial evergreen with stiff, dark green needles held in pairs. Young trees form a dense pyramid, while older trees develop a broad, rounded or flattened crown above stout branches. Brown cones point outward from the shoots, and mature bark becomes deeply furrowed. Native across parts of southern Europe, northwest Africa, and western Asia, it has been widely planted for screens and windbreaks. Its paired needles are a practical first clue, while cone and bark details help distinguish it from other pines.

proposedDescription: Austrian yellowcress is an upright perennial with small, four-petaled yellow flowers and toothed leaves that clasp the stem. Rounded seed pods follow the flowers. It can spread through both seeds and creeping roots, allowing patches to expand in damp fields, pastures and river margins. In parts of the western United States, dense growth can compete with other vegetation, including desirable pasture plants.

previousDescription: Austrian yellowcress is an upright perennial in the mustard family, with small four-petaled yellow flowers and toothed leaves that partly clasp the stem. Its nearly round seedpods help separate it from mustards with long, narrow pods. It grows along moist riverbanks and in disturbed places such as pastures, roadsides, and fields. Creeping underground roots allow a patch to expand as well as spread by seed. In parts of the western United States, it competes with desirable forage and native vegetation.
